images.caption: Base of Central Falls viewed from the Cave of the Winds tour beneath Niagara Falls. The Arrases visited Niagara Falls upon their return from Europe in 1913. Edmund F. Arras (7/7/1875-10/19/1951), a prominent Columbus businessman and entrepreneur, founded one of the city’s first property rental agencies in 1892. Trained as a lawyer, he graduated from OSU law school in 1896 and went on to hold positions in numerous civic groups around the city. He was particularly active within Kiwanis International and was involved with several local religious organizations. In 1913, he and his wife Elizabeth traveled to the World Sunday School Association Convention in Zurich, Switzerland. They continued on to travel extensively throughout Europe documenting their journey through photographs. Due to the timing of their trip, these photos comprise a valuable collection of images of European cities later devastated by war. The Arras family’s lantern slides and negatives include images from their 1913 travels through US east coast cities, Atlantic islands of the Azores, Madeira, Gibraltar and the countries of Algeria, Italy, Switzerland, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, France, England, and Ireland. Also included are images from their 1920 train journey from Chicago to the western US for the Kiwanis Convention in Portland. These photographs include images of Chicago, Denver and western National Parks.

images.filename: Lewiston Municipal Building - fmr Lewiston High School (aka "The Red Brick Schoolhouse") - Lewiston, New York - 20200730.jpg
images.caption: The so-called Red Brick Schoolhouse, 145 North 4th Street, Lewiston, New York, July 2020. A handsome building indeed, the front façade of this two-story beauty is dominated by a large central tower, framed by brick quoins and topped by a tent-roofed octagonal cupola. Round-arched windows (as well as one oculus) on the tower contrast with the segmental-arched windows of the building itself, but ubiquitous are the decorative brick corbelling and ornamental keystone voussoirs adorning the fenestration (save on the ground floor, where simpler splayed lintels predominate). All of this adds up to an interesting early iteration of the Colonial Revival style, tempered with Romanesque Revival influences that are more familiar ground for architect John H. Coxhead. The building served as a school for most of its existence; first it was Lewiston High School (superseded in 1950 by the current Lew-Port High School in Youngstown), then as an elementary school, then for a time as the public library. It's now the home of the village's municipal offices, as well as the Lewiston History Museum and a bevy of recreational programs that take place in the former gymnasium.
